name: Wrike
tagline: Configurable work management with a space hierarchy, structured request forms, and roll-up reporting.
description: Wrike is configurable work management: spaces and folders hold the work, request forms turn intake into tasks, and reporting rolls up projects.
pros: Request forms make intake structured work, so demand arrives in the right space instead of as ad hoc messages
Time tracking and resource management sit next to the schedule, which is what professional services and marketing teams are recorded as using it for
Reporting reads the folder and space hierarchy, giving roll-ups across projects rather than only within one
A freemium entry means lighter tracking can start without a paid plan, per this page's recorded pricing model
Rated 4.2 out of 5 from 2,420 reviews in this repository's recorded data
cons: Configuration is an ongoing responsibility: statuses, fields, forms, and folder structure need an owner, and changes ripple into saved reports
The recorded price band is wide, so real cost depends on which tier the configuration a team chooses actually requires
The hierarchy has to be designed before work starts, which makes Wrike slower to stand up than a fixed board or a flat to-do list

features.description: Spaces hold domains of work with folders and projects beneath them, so a program, a team queue, and a single task each sit at their own depth.

features.name: Request form intake
features.description: Forms collect what a task needs up front and file the result in the right space. This repository records request forms as one of the capabilities Wrike is known for.

features.name: Custom workflows and statuses
features.description: An administrator defines how work moves, which this repository records alongside request forms as the configurable core of the product.

features.description: Hours are logged against the work itself. The Asana review held in this repository records detailed time tracking as part of what Wrike offers.

features.description: Roll-ups read folders and spaces rather than only single projects, which is the reporting depth this page's tagline records for Wrike.

content.title: Spaces, folders, and where work is kept
content.body: Wrike keeps work in a hierarchy: spaces hold whole domains, with folders and projects beneath them, so a program, a team queue, and a single task can each sit at the depth they belong to. That hierarchy is where the configurability comes from, because an administrator decides what a space contains and how its items are structured before anyone fills them in. Teams arriving from one shared board often find the setup stage longer than expected. Teams arriving from folders of spreadsheets tend to find the shape familiar, since the object is still a container with things inside it.

content.title: Request forms that turn intake into tasks
content.body: Intake becomes structured work instead of a message in someone's inbox. A request form asks for what the task needs up front and files the result in the right space, which is how demand enters the system consistently. The Asana review held in this repository records Wrike as offering custom workflows and request forms at comparable pricing, and describes it as popular with marketing and professional services teams that need detailed time tracking and resource management. Read together, those entries describe a tool built around recurring internal service work rather than ad hoc projects.

content.title: Time tracking and resource management
content.body: Because the same review records time tracking as part of the appeal, measured work can be compared with the plan instead of being reported separately from it. Resource management follows the same logic: capacity sits next to the schedule, so a manager can see who is committed before accepting another request. For professional services and marketing teams that bill or must justify effort, keeping hours, assignments, and intake inside one configured system is the practical reason to accept the setup cost. It is also the part of Wrike that simpler task lists do not attempt.

content.title: Roll-up reporting across projects
content.body: Reporting is the part of Wrike that this page's tagline puts first, and it depends on the hierarchy underneath: roll-ups read folders and spaces rather than only single projects, which is what lets a manager see several workstreams at once. The surfaces below are the ones a buyer should ask to see during an evaluation, because their depth is what separates Wrike from a shared task list, and because every one of them is a product of configuration decisions made earlier.
items: Roll-ups that read folders and spaces
Status reporting from task to space
Time reports drawn from logged work
Saved filter views for different audiences

content.title: Where configuration turns into upkeep
content.body: The same choices that make Wrike fit a process make it expensive to change. Statuses, custom fields, request forms, and folder structures are maintained by whoever administers the account, and every change ripples through saved reports and automations built on the old shape. Organizations that reorganize often will pay that cost repeatedly. Buyers should also know that the records held here for Wrike are shallower than for some peers: the comparison files carry pricing and positioning but little on how configuration behaves at scale, so that question belongs in a vendor conversation.

content.title: A freemium entry and a wide price band
content.body: This page records Wrike as freemium with a band of $9.80-34.80/mo, and that band is the only price figure in the record. The spread is the point: entry paid plans and deeper configuration sit far apart, so the cost of Wrike depends on which capabilities a team actually turns on. The Wrike alternatives file held in this repository also notes that free alternatives exist for buyers who only need lighter tracking, which is a useful sanity check on whether the paid band is justified at all. Confirm current list pricing with the vendor before a rollout.

content.title: Deployment, and what this repository does not record
content.body: Wrike is delivered as a hosted service, so spaces, folders, and reports live on the vendor's infrastructure and reach people through browsers and clients. Nothing behind this review documents a compliance certification for Wrike and this review will not assert one; readers get that answer out of the vendor’s current documentation. Because Wrike tends to accumulate intake forms, time records, and cross-project reporting, the questions worth pressing are about permission depth inside the hierarchy, audit history for configuration changes, and what export produces if the account is restructured later.

content.title: Wrike against Smartsheet, Basecamp, and Jira
content.body: Smartsheet, compared with Wrike on a page held in this repository, offers a governed grid instead of a configured hierarchy: structure lives in cells, and standardization comes from templates rather than from spaces and forms. Basecamp goes the other way entirely, a fixed project container with message boards, bought to avoid configuration. Jira keeps appearing where agile rituals matter more than intake forms. The Wrike alternatives file names ClickUp, Trello, Airtable, and Basecamp as the closest substitutes on record, which places Wrike in the configurable middle of this field.

content.title: Who should configure Wrike
content.body: Wrike suits mid-market and enterprise groups that run recurring internal work, such as marketing, professional services, and operations, and are willing to have someone own the configuration: spaces, forms, statuses, and the reports built on them. It does not suit a team that wants to start working the same afternoon with no administrator, or a buyer who needs a single confirmed price and a documented compliance record before signing. Everything above is read from this repository's stored records and published product material for Wrike; nobody here has operated a Wrike account. Those records show 4.2 out of 5 from 2,420 reviews.

faqs.question: What are request forms in Wrike?
faqs.answer: Structured intake: a form collects what a task needs up front and files it in the right space. This repository records request forms and custom workflows as core to how Wrike is positioned.

faqs.question: How does Wrike differ from Smartsheet?
faqs.answer: Smartsheet standardizes through a spreadsheet grid with cell formulas and templates. Wrike standardizes through a configured hierarchy of spaces, folders, forms, and statuses.

faqs.question: Is Wrike free to start?
faqs.answer: This page records Wrike as freemium with a paid band of $9.80-34.80/mo, and the Wrike alternatives file held in this repository notes that free alternatives exist for lighter needs.

faqs.question: What kinds of teams are recorded as using Wrike?
faqs.answer: The Asana review held in this repository describes Wrike as popular with marketing and professional services teams that need detailed time tracking and resource management.

faqs.question: Does this repository record certifications for Wrike?
faqs.answer: No. It stores no certification entries for Wrike, so no such claim is made here. Confirm current documentation with the vendor before procurement or a security review.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Steeper than a board-based tool, because the hierarchy, forms, and statuses have to be designed before the reporting layer has anything worth reading
whoShouldUse: Mid-market and enterprise groups running recurring internal work, such as marketing, professional services, and operations, with someone willing to own configuration: spaces, forms, statuses, and the reports built on them.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams that want to start the same afternoon with no administrator, buyers who need a single confirmed list price before procurement, and organizations that require a documented compliance record on file.
